subject: Refrigeration and Air Conditioning
practicalPaper: Paper 3 offers two practical questions of which one is answered in 2 hours for 100 marks; the materials list is released at least two weeks before. Candidates service, test, pipe or install refrigeration and air-conditioning units, take gauge and electrical readings and diagnose faults; where facilities are lacking an alternative paper may require free-hand sketches of tools, circuits and wiring diagrams.

practicals.title: Operating fire extinguishers and applying first aid
practicals.topic: Safety and First Aid in the Workshop
practicals.aim: To identify safety devices and first aid materials in a refrigeration workshop and demonstrate the use of fire extinguishers and simple first aid.
apparatus: CO₂, dry powder and foam extinguishers
Helmet, goggles, safety boots, gloves, overall, apron
safety: Fire demonstrations are carried out only by the teacher in an open area.
Liquid refrigerant causes frostbite: wear gloves and goggles when handling cylinders.
procedure: Identify each item of PPE and the hazard it guards against.
Read extinguisher labels and match them to fire classes.
Demonstrate PASS (pull, aim, squeeze, sweep) on a controlled fire.
Demonstrate first aid for a minor cut, a burn (cool under running water for 20 minutes) and refrigerant frostbite (warm gently with lukewarm water, do not rub).
Show the emergency action for electric shock: switch off first, then help the casualty.
Record the workshop rules.
practicals.expectedObservations: Students correctly select CO₂ or dry powder for electrical fires and follow the first aid steps in order.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A 9 kg dry powder extinguisher discharging in about 18 s releases about 9/18 = 0.5 kg per second, so it must be aimed correctly from the start.
precautions: Isolate electrical supply before tackling an electrical fire.
Restock the first aid box after use.
commonMistakes: Using water on an electrical fire.
Rubbing frostbitten skin.
examTips: List causes of workshop accidents and their prevention.
State the contents of a first aid box.

practicals.title: Energy conversion and change of state of matter
practicals.aim: To demonstrate conversion of mechanical energy to heat and the change of state of ice to water, and to distinguish sensible and latent heat.
safety: Handle the heater and hot water with care.
procedure: Rub your palms together briskly for 20 s and note the warming (mechanical → heat).
Weigh the crushed ice and place it in the beaker with the thermometer.
Heat gently, stirring, and record temperature every 30 s.
Note the temperature while ice is melting and after it has all melted.
Plot temperature against time.
Identify the flat (latent) and rising (sensible) parts of the graph.
practicals.expectedObservations: Temperature stays at about 0 °C until all the ice has melted, then rises steadily. Heat absorbed during melting does not change the temperature (latent heat).
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Latent heat to melt 0.5 kg of ice: Q = mL = 0.5 × 334 = 167 kJ. Sensible heat to warm the water from 0 °C to 20 °C: Q = mcΔT = 0.5 × 4.2 × 20 = 42 kJ. Melting needs about four times more heat than this warming.
precautions: Stir continuously for uniform temperature.
Keep the thermometer bulb off the beaker base.
commonMistakes: Expecting temperature to rise while ice is melting.
examTips: Link latent heat to the evaporator, where refrigerant absorbs heat while boiling at constant temperature.
Label the graph sections clearly.

practicals.title: Measuring temperature and converting scales
practicals.aim: To use different thermometers to measure temperatures in a refrigeration system and convert between Celsius, Fahrenheit, Kelvin and Rankine.
apparatus: Digital thermocouple thermometer with clamp probe
materials: Ice-water mixture and boiling water for checks
safety: Keep probes away from fan blades; avoid hot discharge lines.
procedure: Identify each thermometer type and its operating principle.
Check each in ice-water (0 °C) and boiling water (about 100 °C).
Measure suction line, discharge line, evaporator air and condenser air temperatures.
Record readings in °C and convert to °F, K and °R.
Plot a chart of the temperature scales against each other.
practicals.expectedObservations: Suction line is cold, discharge line hot; all thermometers agree within about 1 °C after calibration checks.
precautions: Insulate clamp probes from ambient air.
Allow readings to stabilise.
commonMistakes: Adding 32 before multiplying by 9/5.
Writing K with a degree sign.
examTips: State the fixed points: triple point of water 0.01 °C, boiling point of water 100 °C, boiling point of oxygen −182.97 °C.
Show every conversion formula.

practicals.title: Using suction and high-pressure gauges
practicals.aim: To connect a gauge manifold to a running system, read suction and discharge pressures and relate them to saturation temperature and the gas laws.
apparatus: Gauge manifold set (compound and high-pressure gauges)
materials: Running refrigeration or split AC unit with service ports
safety: Wear gloves and goggles; refrigerant can freeze skin and eyes.
Never connect the low-side gauge to the high side with valves open.
procedure: Close both manifold valves; connect blue hose to suction port, red to discharge port (if accessible).
Purge hoses briefly as instructed.
Run the system for 10 minutes and read both gauges.
Convert gauge pressures to absolute using the barometer reading.
Use the P–T chart to find the saturation (evaporating/condensing) temperatures.
Compare with normal values and record the performance.
Disconnect hoses quickly to minimise loss.
practicals.expectedObservations: Suction pressure is low and discharge pressure high; saturation temperatures match the expected evaporator and condenser conditions.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Absolute pressure = gauge + atmospheric: 250 kPa(g) + 101.3 kPa = 351.3 kPa(abs). General gas law: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂. With P₁ = 300 kPa(abs), V₁ = 2.0 L, T₁ = 300 K compressed to V₂ = 1.5 L at T₂ = 330 K: P₂ = 300 × 2.0 × 330/(300 × 1.5) = 440 kPa(abs).
precautions: Always use absolute pressure and kelvin in gas law calculations.
Keep hoses and gauges clean and capped.
sourcesOfError: Readings taken before the system stabilises.
commonMistakes: Using gauge pressure in gas law calculations.
Using °C instead of K.
examTips: State Boyle's, Charles' and Dalton's laws.
Name pressure instruments: barometer, manometer, Bourdon gauge.

checkQuestions.explanation: It is used on the suction side.

practicals.title: Measuring the power used by a compressor
practicals.aim: To measure the voltage and current of a running compressor and calculate its power and energy consumption.
safety: Use the clamp meter so live conductors are not disturbed; keep covers on terminals.
procedure: Run the unit for 10 minutes to stabilise.
Measure supply voltage at the socket.
Clamp around the live conductor only and read the running current.
Read the power factor from the nameplate or energy meter.
Calculate power and energy per day.
Compare with the nameplate rating.
practicals.expectedObservations: Running current is close to the nameplate value; starting current is several times higher for a fraction of a second.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: P = V × I × power factor = 230 × 4.5 × 0.85 = 880 W ≈ 0.88 kW. If the compressor runs 10 h a day: E = 0.88 × 10 = 8.8 kWh per day. 1 kW = 1 000 W; 1 kJ = 1 000 J.
precautions: Clamp one conductor only.
Allow the unit to reach steady running.
commonMistakes: Forgetting power factor.
Confusing kW and kWh.
examTips: State units: power in W or kW; heat in J or kJ.
Show formula, substitution and unit.

practicals.title: Tracing the vapour-compression refrigeration cycle
practicals.aim: To identify the components of a domestic refrigerator, trace the refrigerant path and draw the layout of the vapour-compression cycle.
safety: Do not cut or open refrigerant lines.
Unplug before removing covers.
procedure: Locate the compressor, condenser, filter-drier, capillary tube, evaporator and suction line.
Identify electrical accessories: relay, overload protector, thermostat, capacitor (if fitted).
Run the fridge and feel (carefully) or measure temperatures of each line.
Trace the flow: compressor → condenser → drier → capillary → evaporator → compressor.
Draw and label the layout, marking high and low pressure sides.
State the function of each component.
practicals.expectedObservations: Discharge line and condenser are hot, the capillary outlet and evaporator are cold, and the suction line is cool.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Coefficient of performance: a refrigerator removing 300 W of heat from the cabinet while the compressor takes 120 W has COP = 300/120 = 2.5.
precautions: Avoid touching the hot discharge line.
commonMistakes: Placing the capillary tube on the low-pressure side before the drier.
Calling the condenser the evaporator.
examTips: Name the four processes: evaporation, compression, condensation, expansion.
Draw arrows showing refrigerant direction.

practicals.title: Identifying refrigerants and flow controls
practicals.aim: To identify refrigerants from cylinder labels and colours, state their names and formulae, and identify refrigerant flow controls.
apparatus: Refrigerant cylinders (empty or sealed) and labels
Capillary tube, thermostatic expansion valve (TEV), automatic expansion valve (AEV) samples
safety: Never heat cylinders or store them in sun; keep them upright and capped.
R600a (isobutane) is flammable — no flames or sparks.
procedure: Read each cylinder label: refrigerant number, name, safety class.
Note the colour against the older AHRI colour code (still widely seen in Nigeria).
Record chemical name and formula.
Identify each flow control and state where it is used.
Explain how a TEV senses superheat through its bulb.
practicals.expectedObservations: Older colour code: R-22 light green, R-134a light blue, R-410A rose (pink), R-404A orange. Since 2020 many new cylinders are a uniform light grey/green, so the label is the reliable identifier.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Formulae: R-22 = CHClF₂ (chlorodifluoromethane), R-134a = CH₂FCF₃ (1,1,1,2-tetrafluoroethane), R-600a = C₄H₁₀ (isobutane), R-717 = NH₃ (ammonia). R-410A is a 50/50 blend of R-32 and R-125.
precautions: Never mix refrigerants in a system.
Use dedicated gauges for flammable refrigerants.
commonMistakes: Relying on colour alone.
Charging R-22 into an R-134a system.
examTips: State properties of a good refrigerant: low boiling point, non-toxic, non-flammable, high latent heat, ozone-safe.
Explain the operation of TEV, AEV and capillary tube.

checkQuestions.explanation: Colour coding is no longer reliable.

checkQuestions.explanation: Its bulb on the suction line senses superheat.

practicals.title: Measuring humidity with a sling psychrometer
practicals.aim: To measure dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperatures with a sling psychrometer, find relative humidity and compare air before and after an air-conditioner.
safety: Whirl the psychrometer clear of people and objects.
procedure: Wet the wick of the wet-bulb thermometer with distilled water.
Whirl the psychrometer for about 1 minute in the room air.
Read the wet-bulb first, then the dry-bulb.
Repeat until the wet-bulb reading is steady (lowest).
Find RH from the table or chart.
Repeat in the air leaving the AC indoor unit.
Explain the sensible and latent heat removed.
practicals.expectedObservations: The wet bulb reads lower than the dry bulb because of evaporative cooling; the AC outlet air is cooler and drier.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Room: dry bulb 32 °C, wet bulb 26 °C (depression 6 °C) → RH ≈ 62% from the chart. AC outlet: dry 15 °C, wet 13 °C → RH ≈ 80% but much lower moisture content, because water condenses on the cold evaporator (latent heat removed).
precautions: Use clean wick and distilled water.
Read promptly before the wet bulb warms.
commonMistakes: Reading the dry bulb first and allowing the wet bulb to rise.
examTips: Define relative humidity, dew point, sensible and latent heat.
Explain heating, cooling, humidifying and dehumidifying processes.

practicals.title: Servicing a condenser
practicals.aim: To clean and service an air-cooled condenser and estimate the condenser heat load.
materials: Air-cooled condenser (outdoor unit or fridge back)
safety: Isolate power and lock off before cleaning.
Protect electrical parts from water.
procedure: Isolate the supply; remove covers.
Brush off dust and debris; straighten bent fins with the fin comb.
Apply coil cleaner and rinse gently from the inside outwards.
Check the fan blades and motor bearings; clean.
Dry, refit covers and restore power.
Measure air temperature in and out of the condenser and compressor current before and after cleaning.
practicals.expectedObservations: After cleaning, condenser air temperature rise and compressor current fall, showing better heat rejection.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Condenser heat load = evaporator load + compressor work: 2.5 kW + 0.8 kW = 3.3 kW. Heat rejection ratio = 3.3/2.5 = 1.32.
precautions: Do not use high-pressure water that bends fins.
Use non-corrosive cleaner.
commonMistakes: Spraying water onto live electrics.
Flattening fins with a stiff brush.
examTips: Name condenser types: air-cooled, water-cooled, evaporative.
State the functions of the liquid receiver and service valves.

practicals.title: Servicing an evaporator and estimating heat load
practicals.aim: To defrost and clean an evaporator, clear the drain and estimate the heat load for cooling a product.
safety: Isolate supply before opening the unit.
Never chip ice with sharp tools — it punctures evaporator tubes.
procedure: Switch off and allow ice to melt (or use the defrost cycle).
Clean the coil and filters; check fins.
Clear the condensate drain and check water flows freely.
Check the evaporator fan.
Restart and record evaporator air in/out temperatures.
Estimate the heat load to cool a given product.
practicals.expectedObservations: A clean evaporator frosts evenly (fridge) or gives a good air temperature drop (AC); a blocked drain causes water leaks.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Cooling 50 kg of water from 30 °C to 5 °C: Q = mcΔT = 50 × 4.18 × 25 = 5 225 kJ. Over 4 hours: 5 225/(4 × 3 600) = 0.363 kW of evaporator load.
precautions: Do not use sharp tools to remove ice.
Dry electrical parts before restarting.
commonMistakes: Puncturing the evaporator.
Ignoring the drain line.
examTips: Name evaporator types: plate, finned tube, bare tube; flooded and dry expansion.
Show Q = mcΔT and convert kJ to kW.

practicals.title: Cutting, bending, flaring and brazing copper tube
practicals.aim: To cut, bend, flare and braze copper refrigeration tubing to make leak-free joints.
materials: Soft copper tube (¼ in and ⅜ in)
Silver brazing rods (with flux for copper–brass)
safety: Wear goggles and gloves when brazing; ventilate.
Purge with dry nitrogen, never oxygen, while brazing.
procedure: Measure and cut the tube square with the tube cutter.
Ream the end and blow out chips.
Bend with a spring or lever bender to the required angle without kinking.
Slide on the flare nut, clamp the tube in the flaring block and form a 45° flare; check it is smooth and even.
Swage a tube end and braze a joint while purging with nitrogen.
Tighten flare nuts to the specified torque with a drop of refrigeration oil on the flare face.
Pressure-test the joints.
practicals.expectedObservations: Flares are smooth, concentric and crack-free; brazed joints show a complete fillet round the joint.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Minimum bend radius ≈ 5 × tube diameter for spring bending: ⅜ in (9.52 mm) tube → about 48 mm radius. Length of tube in a 90° bend = (π/2) × R = 1.571 × 48 ≈ 75 mm.
precautions: Slide the flare nut on before flaring.
Deburr all cut ends.
commonMistakes: Kinking tube by bending too tightly.
Brazing without nitrogen purge (oxide scale inside).
examTips: Name the tools listed in the syllabus with uses.
Describe ducting and trunking in AC installation.

checkQuestions.explanation: It gives a square, clean cut.

practicals.title: Leak testing, evacuation and charging a system
practicals.aim: To pressure-test a refrigeration system for leaks, evacuate it and charge the correct mass of refrigerant.
materials: Small refrigeration system with service access
Refrigerant as stated on the nameplate
safety: Always use a nitrogen regulator; never connect nitrogen directly at cylinder pressure.
Never use oxygen to pressure-test (explosion risk with oil).
For flammable refrigerants (R600a), no sparks or flames.
procedure: Pressurise with dry nitrogen to the test pressure on the nameplate/manual.
Check joints with soap solution; watch the gauge for 15–30 minutes.
Release nitrogen and connect the vacuum pump.
Evacuate to about 500 microns and hold to confirm no rise.
Weigh in the refrigerant charge shown on the nameplate.
Run the system and check pressures, temperatures and current.
Test electrical polarity, insulation and continuity.
practicals.expectedObservations: No bubbles and a steady pressure confirm a tight system; vacuum holds below about 1 000 microns; the unit cools normally after charging.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Nameplate charge 150 g of R600a. Cylinder on the scale reads 2 350 g before charging, so stop charging when the scale reads 2 350 − 150 = 2 200 g.
precautions: Charge by weight, not by guesswork.
Evacuate long enough to remove moisture.
commonMistakes: Charging without evacuating (moisture and air remain).
Overcharging.
examTips: List the tests: leakage, polarity, insulation, continuity, pressure and efficiency.
Explain why moisture must be removed.

practicals.title: Diagnosing compressor and electrical faults
practicals.aim: To identify compressor terminals by resistance, test windings and diagnose common faults by systematic and observation methods.
safety: Isolate and discharge capacitors before testing.
Do not run a compressor with the terminal cover off.
procedure: Measure resistance between the three terminals.
Identify common (C), start (S) and run (R).
Test each terminal to the compressor body for earth faults.
Test the relay and overload for continuity.
Observe symptoms of a faulty unit (no cooling, short cycling, noisy, tripping) and list possible causes.
Confirm the fault with tests and record the remedy.
practicals.expectedObservations: The highest reading is between S and R; the terminal not in that pair is C; the lowest reading C–R identifies run. Any continuity to the body shows an earthed winding.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Readings: C–R = 3.5 Ω, C–S = 12.5 Ω, S–R = 16.0 Ω. S–R is highest, so C is the remaining terminal; C–R (lowest) is the run winding; check: 3.5 + 12.5 = 16.0 Ω.
precautions: Clean terminals before measuring low resistances.
Test insulation at the correct voltage.
commonMistakes: Identifying C as one end of the highest pair.
Replacing the compressor when the relay is faulty.
examTips: List common faults: leakage, faulty compressor, poor cooling, current leakage, with symptoms.
Explain systematic vs observation diagnosis.

checkQuestions.explanation: It is both windings in series.

practicals.title: Servicing a window air-conditioner
practicals.topic: Basic Tools Used in Refrigeration and Air-conditioning Workshops
practicals.aim: To select the right tools and carry out routine service on a window air-conditioner.
apparatus: Hacksaw, tube cutter, reamer, spring benders (for identification)
materials: Fan motor oil (if oil ports fitted)
safety: Unit is heavy — lift with two people.
Isolate the supply and discharge capacitors before work.
procedure: Identify the basic tools and state their uses.
Remove the front grille and wash the filter.
Slide out the chassis; clean evaporator and condenser coils; straighten fins.
Clean the base pan and drain holes.
Check fan blades, motor bearings and capacitor.
Reassemble, run and measure supply air temperature drop and current.
practicals.expectedObservations: After service, airflow increases, the temperature drop across the evaporator is about 8–12 °C and current is within the nameplate rating.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Return air 28 °C, supply air 17 °C → temperature drop = 11 °C, within the normal 8–12 °C range.
precautions: Protect electrical parts from water.
Do not bend refrigerant tubes when sliding the chassis.
sourcesOfError: Measuring too close to the louvres.
commonMistakes: Running the unit without the filter.
examTips: List the tools and procedure for servicing in order.
Explain why clean coils save energy.

practicals.title: Installing a split air-conditioner
practicals.aim: To install the indoor and outdoor units of a split air-conditioner, connect piping and wiring, evacuate and commission the unit.
safety: Use a secure ladder and harness when mounting outdoor units at height.
Isolate the supply; use correct cable and circuit breaker.
procedure: Choose positions: indoor unit level and clear of obstructions; outdoor unit with good airflow.
Fix the indoor bracket level; drill the wall hole sloping slightly outward for drainage.
Mount the outdoor unit on brackets or a pad.
Run pipes, cable and drain hose together through the hole and trunking; flare and connect pipes, torquing nuts.
Evacuate the indoor unit and pipes with the vacuum pump; open service valves.
Connect the cable to the terminals per the diagram; fit the breaker.
Commission: run, check current, pressures, air temperature drop and drainage.
practicals.expectedObservations: The unit cools quietly with no leaks; condensate drains outside; current is within rating.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: 12 000 BTU/h = 1 ton of refrigeration ≈ 3.517 kW of cooling. Room 4 m × 5 m (20 m²) at a rule-of-thumb 600 BTU/h per m² needs 20 × 600 = 12 000 BTU/h — one 1.5 hp (12 000 BTU/h) unit.
precautions: Slope the drain hose downward without loops.
Keep pipe lengths within the maker's limit or add refrigerant.
sourcesOfError: Unlevel indoor unit causing water leaks.
commonMistakes: Not evacuating the lines.
Over-tightening flare nuts and cracking flares.
examTips: List installation steps in order.
Identify piping/ducting tools named in the syllabus.

practicals.title: Servicing fan motors and testing capacitors
practicals.aim: To service a fan motor used in refrigeration equipment and test its run capacitor.
safety: Discharge capacitors through a resistor before testing.
Isolate supply and lock off.
procedure: Remove the fan motor and blade.
Check shaft rotation and bearing play; clean and oil if oil ports are fitted.
Measure winding resistances and insulation to frame.
Discharge and measure the capacitor; compare with its marked value and tolerance.
Reassemble with the blade correctly positioned; check direction of rotation.
Run and measure current.
practicals.expectedObservations: A good motor turns freely with no grinding; a weak capacitor causes slow running or failure to start.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Capacitor marked 35 µF ±5% must read between 33.25 and 36.75 µF. A reading of 30.1 µF is (35 − 30.1)/35 × 100 = 14% low → replace.
precautions: Replace capacitors with the same µF and voltage rating.
Refit the blade at the same position on the shaft.
commonMistakes: Testing a charged capacitor.
Fitting a lower voltage rating.
examTips: State types and applications of motors used in refrigeration (split-phase, PSC, shaded-pole).
Describe installation and maintenance of motors and generators.

checkQuestions.explanation: Stored charge can shock you and damage the meter.

practicals.title: Calculating heat gain through cold room insulation
practicals.aim: To identify insulating materials and calculate heat gain through an insulated cold room wall.
materials: Samples: glass wool, fibre glass, polystyrene foam, polyurethane foam, wood, cork, bitumen
safety: Wear gloves and dust mask when handling glass wool and fibre glass.
procedure: Identify each insulating material and list its properties.
Measure sample thicknesses.
Look up thermal conductivity (k) values.
Calculate heat gain through a wall using Q = kAΔT/x.
Compare heat gain for different materials and thicknesses.
Describe the procedure for insulating a pipe or cold room, including vapour barrier.
practicals.expectedObservations: Materials with low k and greater thickness give much lower heat gain; foams are the most effective common insulants.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Cold room wall: polyurethane k = 0.035 W/m K, area 20 m², inside 2 °C, outside 32 °C (ΔT = 30 K), thickness 0.10 m. Q = 0.035 × 20 × 30/0.10 = 210 W. Doubling the thickness to 0.20 m halves the heat gain to 105 W.
precautions: Use consistent SI units (m, W, K).
sourcesOfError: k values vary with density and moisture.
commonMistakes: Using thickness in mm without converting to m.
examTips: State the importance of insulation and properties of good insulants.
Explain the need for a vapour barrier on the warm side.

checkQuestions.q: Heat flow through insulation is reduced by

practicals.title: Commercial marketing survey for a refrigeration business
practicals.aim: To carry out a simple market survey for setting up a refrigeration and air-conditioning repair business and analyse the results.
materials: List of households, shops and offices in the area
safety: Work in pairs, with permission, during daylight; respect respondents' privacy.
procedure: Prepare a short questionnaire: appliances owned, frequency of faults, current repairers, prices paid, satisfaction.
Survey a sample (e.g. 40 respondents).
Visit existing service shops to note prices and services.
Tabulate and calculate percentages.
Identify demand, competition and a good location.
Write a short report with a recommendation.
practicals.expectedObservations: Results show the demand for services such as AC servicing and fridge gas recharge, and gaps in existing service quality.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Of 40 respondents, 28 own an air-conditioner (28/40 × 100 = 70%) and 18 service it at least twice a year (18/28 × 100 = 64% of AC owners). Average price quoted ₦8 000 per service.
precautions: Use a fair, representative sample.
Ask clear, unbiased questions.
commonMistakes: Calculating percentages from the wrong base.
examTips: State types and functions of marketing; low-cost marketing ideas (referrals, social media, signboards).
Present results in a table.
